speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising from an answer given me yesterday by the Minister of Justice when I asked him a question with respect to the discrepancy between a court document presented by the Cape Breton Development Corporation and evidence to the contrary as expressed in a letter, and before a parliamentary committee, by Mr. Tom Kent, the responsible officer for that Crown corporation.
I have evidence to substantiate my statement and refute what was said by the Minister of Justice, who told the House he had had this discrepancy investigated. Perhaps I should first quote what the Minister of Justice said yesterday as reported at page 6906 of Hansard in the second column:
I have had a report on the matter which leads me to believe there is no such element present.
I have here a letter dated April 14, 1969, referred to as exhibit E, presented to the court by the Cape Breton Development Corporation and signed by E. C. Cuddy, director of claims and benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, in which a statement is made about preretirement leave as applied to Cape Breton miners. I do not intend to quote the whole letter, but this is part of it:
As mentioned in your sub-plan, payments are not earnings.
It is emphatically stated in this document, used in court, that they are not earnings.
I quote, now, from a letter directed to me by Mr. Tom Kent on April 3, 1973, after the court case had been terminated. The opening paragraph reads:
I think you must be misunderstanding PRL. The payment has always been considered earnings at all times.
Mr. Speaker, there is no question or doubt that the views expressed in court by Devco and those expressed after the court action by the president of that Crown corporation are diametrically opposed.
If this evidence is not enough to convince the minister that the whole system has gone wrong and that the miners of Cape Breton are not getting their due in accordance with the legislation passed in the House in 1967, I can provide the hon. gentleman with details of a discrepancy between the views of the late Mr. Justice Gillis and the Minister of Justice himself. Two points of view expressed in a letter from the minister to myself are diametrically
opposed to what was contained in the judgment handed down by the late Mr. Justice Gillis.
I am prepared to table the letter from Mr. Kent. I am also prepared to table a copy of the document used by Devco in order that these discrepancies may be fully examined by the minister. If the hon. gentleman wishes, I will also table his own letter and the judgment handed down by the late Mr. Justice Gillis so that he may be aware of the discrepancies in them.
During the hearings in the committee the discrepancies which arose were too numerous for me to mention at this time. I refer this matter to the Minister of Justice. What he is supposed to provide in this country is justice for all, not justice for the high-paid employees of this corporation who have taken care of themselves and who have yet to initiate any action to implement the legislation as provided in section 18(a)(1) and 18(a)(2) of the Cape Breton Development Corporation Act. I can provide document upon document, including one of the minister's own, pointing out the discrepancies in this whole affair.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENTED TO COURT BY CAPE BRETON DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION AND EVIDENCE TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
With respect, I suggest to the hon. member and to the Minister of Justice, who have been involved in an exchange of questions and answers for some time in relation to the very important matter which has been raised, that there should not be a debate at this time. The hon. member has raised this matter by way of a question of privilege, but it would be very difficult for the Chair to agree that there is here a breach of parliamentary privilege which ought to be looked into and investigated by a committee of the House.
The hon. member may have a grievance. He says there are discrepancies between statements made or letters which have been written. That is quite possible. But, with respect, I suggest this is not the type of situation which can be cleared up by means of a debate under the guise of a question of privilege. The whole matter to which the hon. member has been alluding has, in the past, been considered by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. If the hon. member has a grievance, as may well be the case, maybe it could be revived in that way. As I said, I respectfully suggest it should be done in some other way than by a debate on a question of privilege.
The hon. member referred to the possibility of tabling documents. The Standing Orders do not provide for this procedure. If the hon. member has documents he would like the minister to see, he can always send them to the minister. Regretfully, I have to inform him that, as he knows, hon. members cannot table documents in the way he is now proposing to do. I would suggest that the documents be forwarded to the minister and that, with the agreement of the Minister of Justice and all members of the House we might for the time being allow the matter to rest on the statement which the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond has made.

October 17, 1973
Privilege, Mr. Lewis

I do not want to make a mountain out of this but it does concern a very important matter of privilege affecting the House of Commons, parliament and all members of parliament. I learned at about two o'clock-I grin a little about it because of events that have happened elsewhere-that we had a bug at our caucus meeting this morning. During the meeting of the caucus the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), who is our caucus chairman, pulled a little mike out from under the table, put it on top of the table, and said to me and to others: "This looks like a bugging device". However, the person responsible for placing that bug there, a journalist working for the CTV network-

No member of parliament, no politician, certainly not a leader of a political party, wants to alienate anybody in the fourth estate or fifth estate, or maybe all four or five estates that they now represent, as I sometimes think. But I believe that the search for news and for spectacular things in the news, particularly as far as television is concerned, should no longer justify and never should have justified the kind of action which is considered by everybody with any sense of propriety to be indecent and anti-social.

I have no motion to move, Mr. Speaker, though I am going to suggest something in a moment. I am not worried about what happened at the caucus or about the publicity it receives. I am certain that the people concerned, when they were honest enough to tell me about it, will be honourable enough to deal with the matter in a way which we will approve rather than in a manner which would be wrong. However, that is not the point. The point is that everyone in this country, every member of the press gallery and every other person concerned ought to know that this parliament will not stand for that kind of behaviour.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the question of privilege raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party. As the Chair is aware, I and other members on this side of the House have spoken to this matter on more than one occasion in the past. Indeed, Your Honour has caused two investigations that I know of to be conducted into allegations that bugging activities were taking place within the confines of the House of Commons and other buildings.
The example that has been exposed by the Leader of the New Democratic Party brings to the fore once again a situation which I, and I am sure all other hon. members, believe to be deplorable in the extreme. I am not satisfied that the activity is not more extensive and is as isolated as the instance which has been mentioned by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, particularly since the evidence which the standing committee examining the bill dealing with this matter has received indicates there have been well over 1,000 instances where telephone taps or electronic interventions on telephone apparatus have been placed by the police forces of this country.
I would go further than the hon. member for York South and suggest once again, particularly in light of the circumstances disclosed here today by him, that Your Honour cause a further investigation to be made into the whole matter of eavesdropping and electronic devices being placed on members' telephones and in offices as well as in their caucus committee rooms. I do not think it is enough that the House simply order the tape to be produced by the offender. This offence is serious enough to require the offender to come before the bar of the House and give an explanation of the whole affair.

Order, please. I suggest to hon. members that at this stage it might not be in order to have a debate on the very important point raised by the hon. member for York South. In any event, it is obvious to the Chair that there is a prima facie case of breach of privilege involving the type of situation which is normally investigated and looked into by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections of the House of Commons. The hon. member for York South proposes a type of action which might better come as a recommendation from the Committee on Privileges and Elections. At the same time, if there is a desire on the part of the House that the motion proposed by the hon. member be put to the House at this time it would have to be done by unanimous consent because it is a substantive motion.
With respect, I would suggest to the hon. member for York South that for an hour or two the matter might be allowed to rest unless he wishes to put the usual motion that the matter be referred forthwith to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. There could be an immediate meeting of the committee and an immediate recommendation perhaps that the action suggested by the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Yukon be taken. It would be more regular if we proceeded on this basis rather than on the basis of the motion suggested by the hon. member for York South.

subsubtopic: LIMITED AND PROHIBITIVE USES OF NATIONAL PARKS
speechtext: After a careful search of records covering the period 1967 to 1973, we can find no instance of any of the traditional "uses" of Canada's National Parks being prohibited in Banff National Park, Jasper National Park, or Waterton Lakes National Park. All types of uses such as riding, boating, fishing, camping, skiing, etc., which were permitted in 1967 are still permitted in 1973. However, in many instances, and for many different reasons, and for varying lengths of time these uses may have been limited. Hiking trails can be used to illustrate this situation. There are many such trails in each of the three parks in question and one of these trails might have been closed because of fire hazard, bear activity, avalanche hazard, overuse, etc. and for varying lengths of time. The work involved in finding out and listing the limiting factors applied to each use in each park would be an expensive undertaking both from the point of view of manpower and financial resources. In view of this, it would not seem to be in the public interest to carry out the necessary research.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation feels that it has a public responsibility to carry U.S. Presidential speeches when these are expected to be of major historical or international significance or are expected to contain information of importance to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising from the answer given, when I was unavoidably absent on Monday, by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in response to my question No. 2414.
For fully three and one-half months my question concerning the Opportunities for Youth program sat unanswered on the order paper, and I rose at one point to draw my question to the attention of the parliamentary secretary.
The refusal of the Secretary of State to supply answers to questions on the order paper within a reasonable time limits the usefulness of putting questions on the order paper in the first place. This minister has made it clear that he will not answer letters from members of parliament concerned about the program. In my case, for example, I wrote the minister on July 23 and September 11, and since that time called his office once or twice in regard to one project. All I have received in the intervening three months is a letter from the minister's liaison officer dated July 30 stating that the minister would be in touch with me "in the near future."
On Monday the minister answered my question on the order paper by refusing to give information to which members of parliament, who ultimately must accept the responsibility for government programs, are entitled. The first aspect of my question, which dealt with grants requested and given within the constituencies of ministers and parliamentary secretaries, was dismissed with the assertion that "OFY does not maintain statistics on grants by constituency."
In my hand, Mr. Speaker, I am holding a copy of the applications sent me by the minister last April 2 in which he included a memorandum, sent to me, requesting my comments and stating that the bundle represented "copies of the summary sheet of all submissions concerning your constituency." It is quite apparent that the applications were sorted out by constituency. The minister's memorandum which was addressed "To all Members of Parliament," and his assertion earlier this year that members of parliament would be requested to comment on applications from their constituencies, should leave no doubt of that fact. Yet the minister on Monday informed this House that no such data is available. No doubt there are bound to be errors in the sorting of applications by constituency, but the minister did not even bother to try to provide the information and his answer only served to mislead the House.
The second aspect of my question that was dismissed by the minister was my request for the names of the people who acted as references or contact people for applications who also were made members of the local advisory boards passing on their projects, and further information concerning the acceptance or rejection of their projects. The minister's reply to me was that, "Information is not available as to the number of reference or contact people involved with the making of OFY applications who were also members of a local advisory committee."

No answer could be more patently incorrect unless this multimillion dollar program is so incompetently organized that the department does not know to whom money is given or on whose advice it is given. Unless, after sending copies of this information to each of the members of parliament concerned, the department mysteriously destroyed the information for some unknown reason, this data is still available. Indeed, the minister sent me the relevant information for my constituency, and I have it here in my hand.
In two instances the reply given on Monday by the minister was demonstrably false and he has misled the House, albeit unintentionally, with his sloppy and inadequate responses. As a member of parliament, and as a member of the standing committee responsible for overseeing the administration of Opportunities for Youth, I believe that my rights to obtain important information have been abridged by the minister's answer, and it is for that reason that I rise on this question of privilege.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I hope he is in a position to give the House specific answers with regard to fuel supplies for the coming winter. Can the minister now answer the question I asked him on September 21? speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATURAL GAS-ASSURANCE OF SUFFICIENT SUPPLY FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA CONSUMERS THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The National Energy Board has taken as a matter of priority the securing of alternate supplies of gas for the West Coast Transmission system in lieu of those lost in British Columbia because of the structural fault in the field.
The West Coast Transmission Company, at the urging of the board, has carried on negotiations with Alberta gas suppliers for access to Alberta gas supplies, both in the northern part of the province and in the southern part as well. I understand that those negotiations are now in progress between the companies. The position we take is that until the situation is clear with regard to alternate supplies we would not move to take action to curtail.
In addition, some of the British Columbia distributors, particularly Inland, have been in conversations with their customers to discuss the arrangement of alternate supplies where dual burning facilities are available to industry within that province. Indeed, the Chairman of the National Energy Board is meeting this afternoon with the Chairman of the British Columbia Energy Commission for the purpose of clarifying the current state of negotiations for alternate supplies and to discuss further steps that will be taken.

And yet all hope is not lost. This progressive society should do its utmost to increase its population through generous incentives which would encourage married couples to bring their contribution to the demographic needs of a comparatively young country so as to give it the population required to meet its objectives.
We are all aware that the birth rate is intimately connected to the economic conditions. Let us take the necessary steps to settle this thorny problem and ensure an adequate well-being to all families.
Since the aim of the production of consumer goods and services is to meet peoples' needs, work and capital are the means to reach this goal. Profit is an incentive aimed at facilitating the work of grown-ups but it should not take too much importance in the life of our society.
This is the origin of all our economic troubles. Although good in itself, profit becomes bad and even harmful when reaching excessive proportions. In our affluent country the richest are becoming richer and richer and the number of poor is increasing daily. This economic unbalance is prejudicial to children, students, the unemployed and the small wage-earners who do not have sufficient income to enjoy our resources comparatively to the prices asked. What makes it so difficult to adjust family allowances to the cost of living and the rise of the gross national product is precisely the fact that we never consider our economy as the activities of the people as a whole, in order to meet their needs. For many years, the members of the Social Credit have been advocating the payment of a stable and guaranteed salary to each Canadian. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party reminds me of the chameleon which continuously changes colour so as to blend into its environment. It is interesting to note how that party responds when it is under pressure in this country. They seem to have come a considerable distance in our direction or in whatever direction protests come from. I recall the 1940s when the CCF party first won an election in Saskatchewan and came very close to it in Ontario. It went ahead of the Liberal Party nationally at the polls. I remember the era when family allowances were first introduced, the era when the Wheat Board was first set up when there was a grain crisis. That is why I say the Liberal Party is very much like the chameleon because it makes changes in order to adapt to its environment. Nothing is more indicative of this than watching these fellows since last October 30 and seeing the legislation that is brought before the House. It is indicative of the chameleon-type attitude of these people.
Last year they brought in a very complex family allowance bill which contained a means test. Family allowances were supposed to go up or down according to age, sex, family income, and so on. That bill was so complicated that it would have made the Unemployment Insurance Act look simple. Our party objected strenuously to it and said it was unrealistic. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hel-lyer) also objected strenuously to that bill. We said it should be a universal bill, that it should not contain a means test and that the rates should be increased.
According to government members at that time, those demands were unrealistic and impossible. That was prior to October 30. Now, suddenly we find the Liberal Party accepting our ideas. They have brought in a bill that is universal, that provides more money for the families of this country and that is sound in principle. It is interesting to watch the Liberal Party. That is why I was so pleased the other day when I saw the popularity of that party drop down to 35 per cent in the public opinion poll.
Perhaps that chameleon party will be bringing forth some more progressive legislation as they sink lower in popularity. When they sense danger, they respond. Perhaps that is the best hope we have until our party or other progressive elements in the country can form a government that is truly representative of the needs of the people. But the Liberal Party has always fascinated me and I think the legislation before us today is really indicative of how they can change their colour so quickly and appear so natural in a different skin. How anyone can do that as neatly and as subtly as the Liberal Party of Canada, I do not know.
As I said already, the bill before us is based on a sound principle. It will put more money into the hands of ordinary citizens by raising the family allowance from an average of $7 a month to an average of $20 a month. I think that is very good in light of the increase in the cost of living which basically hits people living on low income. However, at this stage I appeal to provincial governments
October 17, 1973

from one end of the country to the other not to cut back on their welfare payments because of the increase in the family allowance, using this as a means of saving provincial money. I know that some provinces have already clarified their stand. My own province of Saskatchewan is not going to penalize welfare recipients. It will increase the allowable welfare level so that family allowance is not deducted.
I would like to see all provincial governments do this, including the Conservative government of the province of Ontario which up until now has hesitated to make this decision. I know that the Ontario minister of social services says his province is considering it, and I think this House should say to him and to all provincial governments that they should not take advantage of this bill in order to cut back on provincial welfare payments; otherwise the increase in family allowances would be quite meaningless to many people.
As I say, this is a good piece of legislation. It is based on a sound principle. But as parliamentarians we should not be carried away, slapping each other on the back, pontificating about what great guys we are and that we are doing such a lot for the people of Canada. Basically this bill will do very little to redistribute income in Canada. It will do very little to assist lower income people meet the cost of living which has gone up faster this year than in any year since the Korean war. As politicians we must not become smug and patronizing toward the ordinary citizen, because really the ordinary citizen is not getting a very decent break at all. To understand this, all one has to do is refer to the statistics mentioned in this House previously which show the distribution of income in Canada.
We find that in the last 20 years income distribution has stayed approximately the same for both the poor and the wealthy. In 1951, the lowest 20 per cent of the population, in terms of income, received only 6 per cent of the disposable income in Canada. In 1971, the lowest 20 per cent received only 7 per cent of the disposable income. In other words, over 20 years, despite all our social plans and programs, the lowest 20 per cent income bracket families have received only 7 per cent of our disposable income. In 1951, the highest 20 per cent of the population, in terms of income, received 41 per cent of the disposable income. In 1971, that 20 per cent received 39 per cent of the disposable income. In my opinion they still receive a much greater proportion of disposable income than they should, despite the large number of social plans which we have, despite programs such as the family allowance program which basically and essentially is a very good one.
I would like to remind hon. members that the Senate Committee on Poverty stated that 4 Vz million poor people in Canada are living in poverty, and of them 1.7 million are children who are deprived of decent nutrition and cannot develop in a healthy manner because they do not have a decent diet. This is something that will affect those children and the families to follow in the years to come.
We should reject some of the insinuations made in this House by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Mac-quarrie) who referred to this legislation as a welfare type of hand-out measure. Mr. Speaker, it is not a welfare measure. It should be viewed as a measure that is helping the children of the country, that is helping in a small way
Family Allowances
to redistribute income and wealth all across Canada. As I say, it is only a small step in that direction. Much more has to be done. The House should seriously consider the idea articulated many times by the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) of paying salaries to mothers who elect to stay at home and look after their families.
For mothers who do not want to stay at home we should be accepting the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women and spending a lot more money right across this country, including provinces which have NDP governments, on day-care centres. By doing so the mother would be liberated in the same way as the man. She could go to work and pursue a career, without being restricted to staying at home and looking after her family, or she could choose to stay at home and look after the family. This type of choice should be allowed in a society as affluent as Canada's. The provision of day-care centres, or of salaries for mothers who elect to stay at home and look after their children would give a great deal more freedom to Canadians in general. This would provide a great deal more initiative to people in terms of exploring their creativity and developing themselves. It would be a boon to the economy by placing more purchasing power in the hands of people who really need it.
As I have said, we should not regard this legislation as being the be-all and end-all. But it is one measure to help redistribute income and wealth. That is the main issue. In some way we must do more for the lower income people by providing them with more funds, with better jobs, by providing retraining, higher minimum wages, more work opportunities in processing and manufacturing industries that are labour-intensive and have potential in terms of growth, and by encouraging the average citizens to form and organize trade unions so that their points of view will be represented at the bargaining table, where presently one-third of the work force is represented, that third being the highest paid segment.
These are things that must be done if the ordinary lower income citizen is to receive a greater portion of the income pie in Canada. For people at the top of the income scale who make their money through dividends, capital gains on the stockmarket or other speculation we should have a more progressive taxation system so that they would not see their incomes go up by leaps and bounds every year despite their being only a small proportion of the population.
Along with all this we need strong governmental action in other areas to protect our citizens. As I said in the House a few days ago, we need a prices review board that is really tough, that has some guts, to stop the gouging and profiteering in areas that affect families, in areas such as food prices, the price of lumber, fuel and energy. These are the things our party says should be controlled if there is excessive pricing and gouging. In Canada we produce energy, lumber, fuel, iron and copper ore. These should be controlled on a selective basis for the benefit of the Canadian consumer. In these areas we, as federal legislators, can take action and this could have a spin-off effect to help the ordinary consumers and families of the country.

It is in this context that we should look at legislation of this sort, even though it is very good and very progressive. With that, I encourage the provincial governments not to take advantage of this legislation to cut welfare allowances for the very poor and unfortunate. I also encourage the people of Canada to keep on mistrusting the Liberal Party and forcing them into this kind of situation. They are communing with nature and changing their colours as the attitudes and opinions of the people of this country change. It is for us on the opposition side to push them. The minute they become smug is the time they will stop bringing forth legislation such as Bill C-211.

Mr. Speaker, we have been very pleased this week to listen to the statement made by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) concerning the bill on family allowances. At first sight, this bill is most interesting as it aims at increasing the purchasing power of Canadian families. However, when we compare this with the increase in the national product and those granted in several other areas, we must come to the conclusion that the family allowance rates under Bill C-211 are clearly lagging behind. And considering that the initial Family Allowances Act dates back to the '40s, it is clear that what is being proposed now would have been equitable in the early '60s. To allow families to balance their budgets is about the best thing a government can do, for it is obvious that the best investment we can make as administrators is increasing the families' purchasing power. And we know that it is there where it will do the most good. Our families are our best consumers since they have so many needs.
Moreover, we do not even have to wonder about it since we are not dealing with grants nor with allowances following niggardly inquiries but with the recognition of the right to live. And since the right to live is the first of all rights, family allowances should be given priority. And it is a well-known fact throughout Canada and especially in the province of Quebec that most fertile couples would like to have three or four children. But in view of the spiralling inflation and of the number of three-and-a-half-room dwellings built under the aegis of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, people prefer to abstain. Therefore we have to come to the conclusion that it is the present economic situation which is responsible for the sterility of Canadian couples.
Mr. Speaker, it is my firm intention to support this bill. However, I still hope that the hon. minister will make a few changes to it. I feel that the minister which his age and experience should use his prestige to request the Minister of Finance's (Mr. Turner) co-operation.
Going back over the years and especially to 1944 when the national product was $12 billion, one finds out that old age security pensions were $20 per month while family allowances were $6 per month. In 1973, the national product being $114 billion, namely nine times as much as in 1944, we have followed the graph in the case of the 65 year old retired people by granting them $179 per month. That is fine and I am delighted along with all the Canadian people. Nevertheless, the legislation now brought forward by the hon. minister is really not in accordance with the production capacity of this country. As a matter of fact, at page 6238 of Hansard for September 5, 1973, one can find a reply given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to question No. 2488 put by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). I am quoting it:
1.	What percentage of the gross national product was spent on family allowances, as at July 31, 1945?

2.	What percentage of the gross national product was spent on family allowances, as at July 31, 1972?
3.	What percentage of government revenues was earmarked for the payment of family allowances, as at July 31, 1945?
4.	What percentage of government revenues was earmarked for the payment of family allowances, as at July 31, 1972?
As a result of an understanding between the Minister of National Health and the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), it was agreed that the department would provide an answer for 1947, since the statistics were more easily available than those for 1945. Now the answer for No. 3 reads as follows:
3.	For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1947, expenditures on family allowances were 8.99 per cent of federal government revenues.
As for question No. 4, the answer is as follows:
4.	For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1973, expenditures on family allowances were 2.48 per cent of federal government revenues.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration proposes an increase; it is true, but such are increase will average $20 per child, three times the present amount.
Two and a half multiplied by three only gives 7'A per cent of the federal government expenditures for 1972 compared with the 9 per cent allotted to that item in 1947.
So, I repeat, the Minister of National Health and Welfare would do well in getting the co-operation of all his colleagues of the cabinet in order to review those figures somewhat.
If it is through administrative techniques that our governments have fostered poverty and unemployment, it is also through corrective legislative techniques that they will restore the balance which will favour Canadian families.
Nowadays, the more people work, exploit the natural resources of this country and increase production, the lower the family allowances percentage. It is a fact that Canadian families and particularly those in the province of Quebec live in very difficult conditions. It is obvious that the proposed increase is a good move for the benefit of families mainly due to the fact that these allowances will be taxable and that taxation rates are relatively low; we must conclude that family heads will receive in one hand and give back with the other.
Then, it is with this situation in mind that I think of the co-operation that the minister should obtain from other cabinet members in order to bring about the early reform needed regarding taxation at source.
Considering that the national output reached $114 billion in 1973, or an average of $5,000 per capita, or $25,000 per family of five, I think it would be possible to exempt from taxation all married couples who earn less than $8,000 a year. By doing that we would only leave them the bare necessities, as an enquiry revealed recently that all Canadian citizens earning less than $8,000 a year cannot even dream any more of buying a house.
I would also like to mention the rate of family allowances in all provinces of the country. I think that the bill
Family Allowances
before us allows too much latitude to the provinces and the amount paid should be the same on a national basis.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF FAMILY AND SPECIAL ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words in favour of the bill before the House, and especially about its fundamental value.
I have listened attentively to most of the remarks made by the previous speakers this afternoon concerning the value of the bill before us, and I do not wish to say any more than is necessary on this subject. However I should like to add a few comments which I believe to be of special importance.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the 29th Parliament, in the Speech from the Throne, it was said that the policy of the government contained two important elements: the economic issues and the social issues.
We know that on the economic level, the budget speech of February 19 last brought several solutions to the problems raised. Other departments, under federal-provincial agreements, the departments of Regional Economic Expansion and of Industry, Trade and Commerce, for instance, took appropriate measures. In the social field, it has been announced that the government intended to review all its social policy.
Last April, the new Minister of National Health and Welfare announced in the House his intention to review the whole social security system in Canada over a period of four or five years. Some aspects of the review of the social security system have already been agreed to by parliament as far as older citizens are concerned. In a few weeks or a few months, assistance will be granted to disabled persons, widows and pensioners and the matter now before us, family allowances, will be dealt with.
There seems to be some features of this bill which should be emphasized and recalled to the Canadian public. They are aimed at children up to 18 and this involves about 3,500,000 families throughout the country. From $6, $8 and $10 they are increased to $20 a month per child in most provinces.
It is worthwhile emphasizing the provincial variations which might be made by provinces in the light of their

October 17, 1973
Family Allowances
own priorities as regards age, family size and sometimes both age and family size.
One of the most important features of this new policy at the time of an astounding rate of inflation is the yearly escalation of those benefits. As you know, the new family allowances will escalate with cost of living. Because of inflation which exists not only in Canada but in most countries of the world, and which is hardly manageable even with supposedly adequately flexible structures, this tie in with consumer prices will be definitely a major factor and the most important aspect of this new social policy.
As you know, social benefits were established in 1945 for children up to 16 and the payments were from $5 to $8 a month. A few minor modifications were made along the years in 1949, 1957, and 1964. As everyone remembers, the 1964 improvement was aimed at increasing the eligibility age from 16 to 17. Perhaps I should add that in 1961, that is, four years before the federal government approved the payment of family allowances in respect of 17 year old children, the Quebec government had already established a school allowance, that is three years before the federal program was approved.
Mr. Speaker, there are in my riding a great many families and families with many children. The unemployment rate is also very high there and, as I stated during the debate on the budget, the high unemployment rate is attributable to the manufacturing industries which are encountering great difficulties. However, Mr. Speaker, I must say that in recent months there was a net improvement in that area but the unemployment rate is still much too high. I think that the bill after being agreed to between the provinces and the federal government will surely be the most important bill to be passed in the last two or three years. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that although it does not solve all the problems of a great number of Canadian families at the low income level that bill represents a definite improvement, and I think it is certainly one of the bills that will have the most effect on Canadian families, on the budget of large families, particularly at a time when inflation is so difficult to control.
There is another point, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to raise; that new social policy is the result of negotiations with provincial governments. The new minister in charge of the Department of National Health and Welfare showed an open mind by listening to the provinces and their priorities with respect to new social security programs in Canada. We are certainly moving toward one of the best organized social security programs in the world; the bill before us is but a step in the revision of the social policy of this country. The new minister in charge of the department made what could perhaps be called a giant step toward the improvement of mechanisms to bring about a greater understanding between the various levels of government in Canada.
In the speech he made in the House when he introduced his bill the minister said and I quote:
In addition, it will advance the development of a more equitable regional redistribution of income across Canada. For these reasons, Bill C-211 represents a major step in the overall reform of the social security system to which this government is firmly committed. As a matter of fact, it constitutes I believe the largest

single federal expenditure ever voted by Parliament for any new program.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is surely one of the most important bills, as far as my riding is concerned at least, and I feel, as regards the provinces that are less fortunate than others, and even the whole country, that this bill will get the support of most Canadian families. I will conclude my comments by quoting the last paragraph of the speech delivered by the minister:
Mr. Speaker, I am personally encouraged by the spirit of cooperation which has been shown by the governments of the provinces toward the review of Canada's social security system. I am confident that given the goodwill that has prevailed to date, we shall be able, within the next few years, to set in place a social security system which will ensure a better standard of life for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with my colleagues- regardless of their party-who will approve this bill. I believe that we must approve it as soon as possible because winter is almost here and a large number of Canadian families would like to see this bill passed without delay so that they can take full advantage of this review of our social security system, in particular as far as family allowances are concerned.

subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURES TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENT OF FAMILY AND SPECIAL ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the House will be pleased with the change that has taken place in the past year with regard to family allowances, and with the fact that we have before us now legislation to provide increases in family allowances on a universal basis. I do not think there will be many complaints about the fact that the minister has seen fit to raise to $12 the benefit immediately in the non-taxable category, and on January 1 to raise the benefit to $20 for all children of all families in Canada up to the age of 18. I am sure that in some provinces this has made a considerable difference, because in some provinces the youth allowances program is different than in others and the program is not universal as is the family allowance program.
I am particularly pleased that the minister does not adopt the male chauvinistic attitude which was made evident in his province in the last year or so when this matter was discussed and considerable arguments were raised against payments going to the mother. Arguments were being put forward in favour of the father receiving the money. It seems to me that the present arrangement is excellent for the Women's Lib movement. The children get the $20 through the payment to the mother, the mother gets the money and the father pays the tax on that money. It seems to me to be a fairly good arrangement.
However, I am concerned-and other members of the House have expressed this concern-about two or three other problems which have not been given much consideration. One of them is a problem which we have not faced, and which we are certainly not facing in this piece of legislation. I am referring tc payments to the young person-here I am not referring to those up to 18 who continue their education but, rather to those beyond the age of 18-whose need for financial assistance to continue his or
October 17, 1973

her education becomes considerably greater and for whom no arrangement has been made in many of the provinces.
All provinces administer a program of student loans for education, but the need of young people for special assistance to enable them to continue their education has not been met. Loans and assistance are given in relation to the income of the father and the mother of these young people as well as any other income that may come into the family. The expenditures which families may have are not taken into consideration, nor is another important factor taken into condideration, namely, whether or not the young person wishes to remain under the care of the family.
I am sure that all hon. members know that if a young person is married, he or she does not qualify for provincial assistance in the form of loans or grants for education in all the provinces. The requirement is for them to be in the labour market for a period of time which is different in various provinces. It does not seem to me that because a young woman does not feel happy living at home and does not get along too well with her family, and certainly does not receive any money from her family, it is fair that in considering her application for assistance to continue her education the government should consider the income of the family, il know of several young women who have married for the simple purpose of gaining independence from their parents. This happens more often in the case of families that are well off than in the case of families in the middle or lower income group.
Another aspect which may not meet with approval from all members of the House is that when family allowances are increased, welfare payments may be cut accordingly. I would like to quote from today's Toronto Star a passage regarding a statement made by Mr. Brunelle in the provincial legislature. It reads as follows:
In the legislature yesterday, Brunelle denied reports that Canada's ten provincial welfare ministers agreed in a closed meeting in Ottawa last week to prevent welfare families from getting the full benefit of the increase.
I am sure the minister does not agree that they should not get the full benefit of the increase. If it had been his position, obviously this plan would not be on a universal basis and we would be again faced with the FISP of last year. The article continues:
Holding up a clipping from the Star, Brunelle said Ontario has not made up its mind but definitely did not agree to abide by a federal government suggestion to keep part of the family allowance raise away from welfare families.
In my area the two groups receiving most advantage from family allowance are the low-income group and the welfare group. In setting the allowable budget for welfare families in Ontario, family allowances should not be included. If they are, then you and I, Mr. Speaker, and every other member of this House are being ripped off. Almost all members of this House agree that we should increase the amount being paid through family allowance to $12 per child immediately, without any income tax provision, and to an average of $20 per child after January 1 next.
Obviously we intend that the mother will get $20 for each child. I understand there has been agreement with the provinces of Quebec and Alberta to vary the amount
Family Allowances
* per child. I have not heard the details but I presume that the younger the child, the less the payment; and the older the child, the more the payment, provided the average remains at $20. But if we are to be told by the Ontario minister of social and family services that he will deduct the $20 family allowance from the budget allowed to welfare families, then I think we had better make this payment in another way. We certainly should not make it in a way whereby the provincial government can benefit from it. That would be dishonest and the public should know about it.

speechtext:
In the province of Ontario, if a person receives workmen's compensation or some federal payment and he lives in a rent-to-income project, his rent can be increased. I know of one family in such a project who paid $36 in rent for an apartment. Then the family was covered by a cost-shared program. It must be remembered that in Ontario the provincial government pays 40 per cent of cost-shared programs, the federal government 40 per cent and the municipality 20 per cent. Anyway, as a result the rent of that apartment went up to $84, even though the cost of the apartment was covered initially by the $36 payment. That is often done in welfare cases.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) should be prepared to introduce an amendment to ensure that the Ontario minister cannot take the increased family allowance out of other welfare payments. Of course, we could increase family allowances to the point where Ontario would not have to pay anything. But, Mr. Speaker, Ontario is not a poor province; it does not have to be niggardly.
This is something that has also been done by the federal government. When old age pensions were increased, the increase was taken off war veterans allowance. A previous minister of veterans affairs could never understand this. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I spent half an hour one day trying to explain it to him. We tried to show him that the veterans would lose money. The present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) has been able to get that point across in cabinet, so that an increase given under one piece of legislation will not be removed under another piece of legislation.
The government must be given full credit for the universality of the family allowance scheme. I will not complain if people who have enough money of their own must pay back some of the family allowance through income tax, but I repeat that it would be a shame if provinces deducted the increase in family allowance from welfare payments. Welfare families constitute the one category that needs assistance above all others. We have all dealt with welfare people. We know that there is a certain percentage of people who, when they receive welfare cheques, may spend them on drink. But the family allowance is paid directly to mothers, and in my experience

October 17, 1973
Family Allowances
they use the money to buy clothes and food for their children.
I certainly do not want to leave the impression that all welfare families take their cheques down to the local liquor store to cash them. That is not true. But it is a fact that many people on welfare have difficulties, mentally, physically and emotionally and in a number of other ways, and are least able to look after their money and to provide for their children. If Mr. Brunelle in the province of Ontario deducts the additional money that will be paid by the federal government now, and in particular after January, the people who will be hurt are the children, the very people whom we are passing this legislation to protect.
Members of this House can say that is a provincial matter, but I am not very sympathetic to the provinces playing around with legislation when we are making the sole contribution. I do not see Quebec's point of view at all. I do not see why Quebec wants a different program from anyone else, and I do not see why Alberta wants a different program. If the province of Quebec feels that the youth allowance should be increased, then they should put some money into it and increase it. That is true for the province of Ontario or any other province. We have the responsibility for all Canadian children and we should provide them with a benefit which is applied all across the country.
If the minister replies, Mr. Speaker, I am sure he will indicate that he has had meetings with the provincial welfare ministers and that they have made it difficult for him to explain this welfare program. I am sure the province of Ontario would like him to give them one large sum of money once a year in lieu of the family allowances, and I am sure most of the provinces would agree to such a proposition and then make their own distribution. But in my opinion it would seldom get to the children and the youth of this country and I am therefore pleased that the minister has agreed to make this program universal. I will be sympathetic with the position he has had to take with Quebec and Alberta.
It may cost less to raise a one year-old child than an 18 year-old child; maybe there is some merit in that argument. I am not prepared to argue that there is not. I have raised children, and in my opinion they were pretty easy to raise when they stayed in the crib; problems did not develop until they started to wander around. Of course, it got worse the more they wandered around; the further afield they wandered, the more expensive it became.
I am concerned about this idea of allowing the provinces to take the low end of the strap, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre congratulated the minister because this is a redistribution of wealth. It is not going to be a redistribution of wealth in the province of Ontario if the minister responsible for social welfare in that province decides he is not going to pass on the $20 payment that we will be making after January, but will deduct it from the amount he has to pay to maintain the young people in the province.
What really concerns me, Mr. Speaker, is that it will be two or three years before there is an election in Ontario. A lot of hardship and sorrow could happen in that time. A

rich province like Ontario could use the $20 or a portion of it to add to the welfare rolls that they would normally have to carry and are in fact now carrying at a specific level. This could mean a reduction in the level. And Mr. Brunelle does not make any bones about it; he says that Ontario has not definitely agreed to abide by a federal government suggestion regarding part of the raise in the family allowance being kept away from welfare families. He says they did not agree, and if they did not it means that he is probably going to take this into consideration as part of the payment.
I come from a wealthy province, but welfare is a problem both for the municipalities and the provincial government in my area. About nine-tenths of the townships I represent are unorganized townships and have no form of municipal government. They therefore come directly under the municipal authorities for welfare and are paid directly by the municipal welfare branch. I am concerned that the families are not going to get the benefit of the payments that we are making.
The minister should give some consideration to the arrangement that we are making in terms of the cost-shared programs which are already operating. We give 50 per cent of that money and then an additional outside payment. The amount the federal government will be paying and the amount the provincial government will be paying into that welfare structure will be decreased by the amount by which we increase the family allowance. If that happens, Mr. Speaker, a lot of people are going to be very unhappy about the role played by members of parliament in providing for the middle-class, and in some cases the upper-class in our society while having neglected to make the full benefit available where it is most needed, at the welfare level.
I have read that the minister says he did not have the meeting, and the provincial minister said that he did. I am sure the deputy minister discussed it or it was discussed at another level. I strongly urge that in addition to the cost-sharing welfare structure, we bring as much pressure to bear as is possible to see that all welfare families in this country receive the full benefit of the federal government's generosity which should be universally available regardless of a family's income or in what province they may reside.

Not until it was explained to me-after all, I do not pretend to be an expert on pensions, taxation and fiscal

policies-did I realize, although my grandfather did not realize it, that he was not paying for that box of cigars with his old age pension cheque. I should like to bring several points to your attention, Mr. Speaker. I have received some correspondence from constituents who complain that they will be taxed at a higher rate because of what they regard as this useless contribution to Canadians. The people, of course, who send these complaints are not in that group of Canadians who will profit from this program. I have received several letters. Actually, I am replying to one now and am explaining to the gentleman that, first, taxes will not be raised. Taxes have been reduced this year. I have tried to explain to this gentleman that, although he may complain, it is increased revenues resulting from this government's management of the economy, or the increase resulting from an expanding economy, which will pay for this program. I said that his taxes were probably
Family Allowances
reduced this year and the program will not cost him any more money. His taxes are not going to be increased. I am not the first to say that this government has given priority to social security legislation. Mr. Speaker, I think the Liberal Party has always made a significant contribution in this area. One has heard during the past while some rather hyperbolic statements about this government and, I suppose, about the Liberal Party. I should like to mention the names of some men who have been responsible for social security legislation in this century. They have been members of the Liberal Party, or of a Liberal Party. As to the ever useful and relevant comments of the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) - [English]
I should like to stress once again that this is, indeed, only a partial measure, only a step toward a complete revision of our social security arrangements. It has not been put forward by the government as being anything else. As I say, it is only a step, though, I believe, a major step in the review and reorganization of our social security system.
We took another step at the recent federal-provincial conference of welfare ministers in which we agreed to make important changes, particularly in the field of pensions under the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. Other steps are to be taken with regard to community employment, income supplementation and the question of a guaranteed income. Working parties are actively engaged in a review of this field at the present time and there is no reason to expect that this joint review will not be completed before the deadline which the government has set itself. We are going ahead as fast as
October 17, 1973

human resources will allow and I hope that our two-year deadline will be met in ample time.
The next step, the hon. member said, is to control the means of life in this country, and she mainly related this to control of large corporations. This is a subject that is outside my jurisdiction but certainly one which is being considered and discussed. It is in this regard that the government undertook certain steps recently in connection with beef and pork. We have even taken steps with regard to oil. However, it seems to prove that the big problem may not only lie with large corporations but also with large provincial governments. I hope the hon. member will give her support to the government when and if it becomes necessary for the federal government to exercise its true responsibility for the national interest of this country.
Finally, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said that if the provinces want to change the family allowance configuration they should do so by using their own money. I think there are two points to be made here. The act provides that the provinces can modify the federal plan according to age or number of children. As I have stated, two provinces have indicated that they will do so, namely, Alberta and Quebec. In addition, Prince Edward Island has decided to supplement the plan with their own money.
I wish to point out that both Quebec and Prince Edward Island are adding substantial funds to the federal family allowance scheme. Quebec is adding roughly $100 million of its own money through its own family allowance scheme to supplement the amount being provided by the present legislation. As for Prince Edward Island, it has decided to use the funds coming into the province by way of income tax transfers as a kind of windfall gain so that the province, through fiscal arrangements with both the federal and provincial governments, can effect an increase in family allowances of $10 for the fifth and subsequent children. So this province, too, will effectively use money coming back to it via income tax transfers to increase family allowances.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the few points I wanted to make. The committee will have an opportunity to go into the details of the bill. As the hon. member for Hillsborough has said, various new initiatives and aspects are put
Family Allowances
forward in the bill which deserve thorough examination. If the committee so wishes, I shall certainly be pleased to make myself and my officials available to the committee in order to discuss the points that have been raised. I might also say that in all likelihood I will have a few amendments to propose at the committee stage.
I listened with great interest to the contributions and suggestions made by the various members of the House regarding the bill. As a result of the two meetings I have had with my provincial colleagues, further suggestions have been made for improving or refining the bill. I hope that when these proposals are put forward at the committee stage they will receive the same degree of support that this bill in general seems to have in the House at the present time.
I should like to conclude with those remarks and I once more thank hon. members for their contributions to this debate.
